question:
Patient note:
A 67-year-old man is evaluated this morning in the ambulatory procedure suite just before a planned outpatient excision of a 1.8-cm hyperkeratotic plaque on the left forearm that dermatologic surgery classifies as a brief, superficial operation expected to last under half an hour with monitored anesthesia care and a same-day discharge. He drove himself to the hospital, parked on the fifth level of the garage, walked the two city blocks to registration, and ascended a flight of stairs to the waiting area without shortness of breath or need for assistance, noting that he still completes a brisk mile on the treadmill every other evening despite mild airflow limitation. Past medical history is notable for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease related to a 45-pack-year cigarette exposure; he quit nine years ago and now manages occasional exertional wheeze with once-daily tiotropium and an albuterol inhaler that he keeps in his gym bag but rarely uses. Pulmonary follow-up six weeks ago documented an FEV₁ of 70 % predicted, no recent exacerbations, and no need for home oxygen, mechanical ventilation, or systemic steroids. Two years earlier he was diagnosed with moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon after a screening colonoscopy revealed a friable mass; he underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic low-anterior resection followed by adjuvant CAPOX chemotherapy that finished nineteen months ago. Surveillance imaging performed last quarter showed no evidence of recurrence, but the oncology team continues twice-yearly intravenous bevacizumab infusions administered through a right-sided subcutaneous port-a-cath placed fourteen months back; the reservoir is palpated today beneath intact skin, the dressing is dry, there is no erythema or tenderness along the catheter track, and brisk blood return was documented when the oncology nurse accessed it yesterday for pre-procedure laboratory draws. He reports no other operations, endoscopic procedures, or invasive radiologic interventions in the last thirty days, and has not required urgent or emergent admissions during that interval. He denies fevers, chills, sweats, rigors, productive cough, sputum change, or clinician-diagnosed pneumonia since last winter, and has not experienced dysuria, abdominal pain, or altered mental status suggestive of systemic infection. Cardiovascular review is negative for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, exertional chest discomfort, palpitations, or presyncope; the most recent transthoracic echocardiogram, obtained during hypertension work-up eight months earlier, showed preserved biventricular function with an ejection fraction of 60 % and no valvular abnormalities. He has never been told he has weak heart muscle, fluid overload, or decompensated failure and cannot recall taking loop diuretics. He has avoided falls, motor-vehicle collisions, or high-energy injuries and therefore has no history of fractures of the pelvis, hip, or long bones, nor has he worn splints, slings, or casts in recent memory. Neurologically he denies focal deficits, transient ischemic events, or paralytic syndromes, and he ambulated into the clinic with a steady gait. There is no prior episode of clot in the legs or lungs; Doppler sonography has never been ordered, and chest imaging across multiple CT scans for cancer surveillance has never commented on filling defects in the pulmonary arteries. He recalls no relatives who developed venous thromboembolism at a young age or after minor provocation. Current medications, all taken as prescribed, include tiotropium 18 µg inhaled each morning, albuterol 90 µg two puffs as needed (last dose three weeks ago), lisinopril 20 mg daily, and low-dose aspirin that he stopped five days ago at the surgeon’s request; he does not use glucocorticoids, hormone replacement, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antiplatelet drugs other than the aspirin. He drinks a glass of red wine with dinner on weekends, denies illicit substance use, and maintains a body mass index of 26 kg/m². On examination he sits comfortably on the stretcher, converses in full sentences, and is in no distress. Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II with good cervical extension and intact dentition. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Lungs are clear to percussion with faint end-expiratory wheezes bilaterally but no crackles. Abdomen is soft, well-healed from prior laparoscopic ports, and nontender. Inspection of both lower limbs shows flat, uniform skin without visible varicosities, pitting edema, erythema, or calf circumference difference; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric, and gentle dorsiflexion elicits no discomfort. Neurologic screening demonstrates full orientation, 5/5 strength, and intact sensation. A single 20-gauge peripheral intravenous catheter placed in the left antecubital fossa is running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate in addition to the indwelling chest port that remains capped and heparin-locked. Pre-operative laboratories from yesterday reveal hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, platelets 232 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 6.7 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, AST 24 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.2 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 72 beats min⁻¹ with flat lateral T-waves unchanged from prior tracings, and a chest radiograph obtained during cancer surveillance three weeks ago demonstrates clear lung fields, stable mild hyperinflation, and the catheter tip terminating at the cavo-atrial junction without malposition. Sequential pneumatic compression devices are at bedside but will not be activated until the sterile field is established, and no anticoagulant prophylaxis has been started pending completion of the surgical time-out.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini surgical VTE risk score sums the patient's weighted risk factors before surgery:
- Age 61–74 years: age 67 → 2.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 26 → 1.
- Minor surgery: superficial excision expected to last <30 minutes → 1.
- Chronic lung disease: documented COPD → 1.
- Current or previous malignancy: sigmoid adenocarcinoma → 2.
- Central venous access: the indwelling chest port qualifies even when capped → 2. The peripheral IV adds no points.
No additional qualifying factors are documented: he is mobile and has no prior VTE, known thrombophilia, recent major surgery, or lower-limb fracture.
Total = 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 9.
Final answer: 9
